Flat Disk
Geometry Modeled

How this far-field detector answers off-axis, near-field and uncertainty-aware queries.

  • Flat Disk - the classic far-field model: efficiency is the on-axis curve scaled by solid angle, with an energy-correlated uncertainty you edit on the Anchor tab. No geometry is modeled.
  • Geometry Modeled - a Monte-Carlo response, built from the detector geometry below and grounded to the efficiency points on the Anchor tab, supplies the distance/angle dependence and its own finer uncertainty.

Switching a geometry-modeled detector back to Flat Disk detaches its response on "Use" (you will be asked to confirm).

The detector's measured efficiency points, which are also what its efficiency curve is: the absolute efficiency at the reference distance below. Edit each point - its energy, efficiency, and the statistical and certificate uncertainties on that efficiency. "Stat. %" is independent from one point to the next; "Cert. %" is the source activity uncertainty, and points sharing a source are treated as sharing it.

The peaks this detector was characterized from: the absolute efficiency measured at each source's own distance. The efficiency equation is re-fit from these points when you press "Use", so the curve, its covariance and these points always describe the same detector - editing a point therefore moves the curve, and editing only an uncertainty changes how strongly that point pulls on the fit. "Stat. %" is independent from one point to the next; "Cert. %" is the source activity uncertainty, shared by every point of the same source.

The detector's efficiency points and their uncertainties, which the Activity/Shielding fit can fold into its results. Each point's uncertainty is split in two: "Uncorr. %" is the part that is independent from one energy to the next (Monte-Carlo convergence, counting statistics), and "Corr. %" is the part that moves together across energy (a baseline modeling uncertainty, for instance). How far that "together" reaches is set by "Correlated part, across energy" below. A blank cell means none.

The efficiency equation exp( A0 + A1*log(x) + A2*log(x)2 + ... ) and the covariance among its coefficients, which the Activity/Shielding fit can fold into its results. The diagonal is the 1-sigma uncertainty of each coefficient (absolute, not a percent - these are logs), and the off-diagonal is the correlation between them. Fitted coefficients are strongly correlated, so the off-diagonal matters as much as the diagonal.

The efficiency formula, with energy as x, and its uncertainty. The formula gives the efficiency, so the rows below are uncertainty only: one row per energy you want to state one at, split into the part that is independent from one energy to the next ("Uncorr. %") and the part that moves together across energy ("Corr. %"), as an ISOCS .ecc file does. For one flat uncertainty at every energy, give a single row. These rows ARE the uncertainty: clearing their percentage columns says the detector states none.

This detector answers every efficiency and uncertainty question through its geometry-modeled response. The numbers below are what that response is built from; it is rebuilt from them when you press "Use".
At {1} keV this detector reports an efficiency uncertainty of {2}%, all of it from its own data.
At {1} keV this detector reports an efficiency uncertainty of {2}%: {3}% from its own data, {4}% model envelope.

At {1} keV this detector reports an efficiency uncertainty of {2}%, none of which is a measurement of this detector: {3}% is a default for a detector that never stated one, and {4}% is the model envelope. Enter what you know about it above.
This detector reports no efficiency uncertainty, so analyses using it will report only counting statistics.

The fractional efficiency uncertainty the Activity/Shielding fit would propagate, at one representative energy - the same number the band on the efficiency chart is drawn from.

It can read lower than any single number in the table above, and that is not a mistake: between two stated energies the uncertainty is interpolated, so a part that is independent from one energy to the next partly averages out in between (by up to a factor of √2 exactly half way). A part that moves together across energy does not.

From its own data is measurement: counting statistics, source certificates, and the fit or Monte-Carlo statistics behind the curve. More or better data shrinks it. Typically 0.3 - 5%.

Model envelope is an allowance for the model being asked about a position nobody measured - a few tenths of a percent on axis and far away, 1.5 - 2.5% for a Monte-Carlo response's regime floor, and up to 10 - 25% very close in or well off axis at low energy. It does not shrink with more counting, and it is the same error for every peak at once. A detector with no measured uncertainty at all (a GADRAS Detector.dat) reports about 5% here that is purely this kind of allowance.

These uncertainties and correlations cannot describe any real set of errors (the matrix is not positive semi-definite). Left as they are, the analysis would quietly fall back to counting statistics alone - so they have to be corrected before this detector can be used. Usually one correlation is too strong given the others.
